For robust intent classification in chatbots, the papers point to a few complementary strategies: use models and evaluations that explicitly test perturbation robustness [1], prefer attention pooling over mean pooling when user messages contain conversational noise like greetings or off-topic remarks [2], and consider training-free methods if you expect mixed-intent or adversarial prompts, since they are generally more robust in those settings [3]. For multi-intent spoken interactions, a semantic-frame self-consistency method improves overall accuracy and slot F1, though intent accuracy stays mostly stable [6].

If robustness includes unknown or out-of-scope intents, open-intent methods are relevant: ellipsoid-based decision boundaries improve open intent detection and generalization [4], while uncertainty estimation for open-set text classification helps predict recognition errors and reject unknowns, including on intent datasets [10]. For multilingual customer-service chatbots, translated benchmarks can overestimate robustness on noisy native queries, so realistic native-query evaluation is important [7].
